title: Design a Distributed Unique ID Generator (Snowflake)
tagline: Generate billions of unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit IDs per day across many machines — no coordination per ID.
summary: Why not UUID/auto-increment; the Snowflake 64-bit layout.

items.detail: Globally, across many servers and data centers, with no duplicates.
Newer IDs > older IDs (useful for ordering feeds, pagination, and DB index locality).
Fit in 64 bits (a BIGINT), so they're small and fast to index/store.
Generate 10,000+ IDs/sec per node without coordinating with other nodes on each ID.

sections.title: 2. Why the obvious options fall short

rows: Single point of failure + write bottleneck; doesn't scale across DBs; sequential = guessable
Unique & decentralized, BUT 128 bits (big), not time-sortable, and random → terrible DB index locality (page splits)
Single coordinator per ID = latency + SPOF unless made HA

blocks.text: UUIDs are fine when you just need uniqueness and don't care about ordering or size. But for IDs used as primary keys / sort keys at scale, their randomness hurts index performance and they're 2x the size. That's the gap Snowflake fills.

paragraphs: Twitter's **Snowflake** composes a 64-bit ID from several parts, so each machine generates IDs locally with zero coordination, yet they're globally unique and time-ordered. A common layout:

rows: Gives ~69 years of millis and makes IDs time-ordered
Up to 1,024 unique generators (data center + worker)
Up to 4,096 IDs per machine per millisecond
blocks.caption: 41 + 10 + 12 = 63 bits (+1 sign). Each machine: timestamp + its id + a per-ms counter → unique without talking to anyone.

paragraphs: How a node generates one: take the current millisecond, append its assigned machine id, and append a sequence counter that increments within the same millisecond (resets each ms). 12 sequence bits → 4,096 IDs/ms/machine = ~4 million IDs/sec/machine. The leading timestamp makes IDs monotonically increasing over time, so sorting by ID ≈ sorting by creation time.

codes.title: snowflake.py

items.detail: If a machine's clock moves backward, you could generate a duplicate/out-of-order ID. Handle by refusing to generate until the clock catches up, or by waiting. This is the classic Snowflake gotcha.
Each generator needs a unique worker id. Hand them out via a coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd) or config; reusing an id breaks uniqueness.
If a machine exhausts 4,096 IDs in one ms, it waits for the next millisecond — fine, since that's 4M/sec/machine.
IDs are time-ordered to the millisecond, but two IDs in the same ms from different machines aren't strictly ordered. 'Roughly sortable' is usually enough.

blocks.text: The crisp summary: '64-bit ID = timestamp + machine id + per-ms sequence. Each node generates locally (no coordination), IDs are unique and time-sortable. Main risk is clock skew — guard against backward clock moves.' That's a complete answer to the common 'design a unique ID generator' question.

cheatsheet: Need IDs that are globally unique, time-sortable, 64-bit, and generated locally without per-ID coordination.
Auto-increment = SPOF/bottleneck; UUIDv4 = unique but 128-bit, unordered, bad index locality.
Snowflake 64-bit = sign(1) + timestamp(41) + machine id(10) + sequence(12).
Each node: ms timestamp + its machine id + per-ms counter → ~4M IDs/sec/machine, time-ordered, no coordination.
Watch clock skew (refuse/wait on backward clock); assign unique machine ids via ZooKeeper/etcd.

questions.prompt: When is a UUID perfectly fine, and when does Snowflake-style ID become worth the extra complexity?
questions.hint: Think size, ordering, and how the ID is used in storage.
answer: A UUID (v4) is perfectly fine when you just need a globally unique identifier generated anywhere with zero coordination and you don't care about ordering or size — e.g., request/trace ids, idempotency keys, opaque external references. It's the simplest correct choice there.

Snowflake becomes worth it when the ID is used as a **primary/sort key at scale** and you want time-ordering and compactness: 64-bit IDs index far better than random 128-bit UUIDs (random keys cause B-tree page splits and poor cache locality), and time-sortable IDs let you order/paginate feeds by ID directly. So: UUID for opaque uniqueness; Snowflake when storage performance and ordering matter.
keyPoints: UUID: simplest, fine for opaque uniqueness without ordering/size concerns
Snowflake: 64-bit, time-ordered, better index locality for PKs at scale
Random UUID PKs hurt B-tree/index performance
Choose based on whether ordering + storage cost matter
followUps: Why specifically does a random primary key hurt a B-tree index?

questions.prompt: A Snowflake node's clock is corrected backward by NTP. Why is this dangerous and how do you handle it?
questions.hint: The timestamp is the high bits of the ID.
answer: The timestamp forms the high-order bits of the ID. If the clock jumps backward, the node could regenerate timestamps it already used, and combined with the sequence counter that risks producing a **duplicate ID** (or at least an out-of-order one that violates the time-sortable guarantee).

Handle it by tracking the last timestamp used: if the current clock reading is *less* than the last one, the generator must not emit IDs with the older timestamp. Options are to **wait** until the clock catches up to the last timestamp before generating again, or to **reject/alert** if the skew is large. Some implementations keep a monotonic 'last max timestamp' and only advance forward. The key point in an interview is recognizing clock skew as the primary correctness risk of Snowflake and proposing a forward-only/wait strategy.
keyPoints: Timestamp = high bits → backward clock risks duplicate/out-of-order IDs
Track last-used timestamp; never emit with an older one
Wait for clock to catch up, or reject/alert on large skew
followUps: How would you assign and manage the 10-bit machine IDs across hundreds of nodes?
